method.record_universe: Every retained Wave 06 record. The FBI technician, FBI analyst, and Neil Jacobs matters receive stage-level review; reclassification-without-consequence, policy-defect, lawful-discipline, stay, and anti-gag records receive control-level review.
method.chain_rule: provisional_ccd_chain_depth is the deepest uninterrupted documented stage beginning at stage 0; it is null when stage 0 is not documented.
method.furthest_rule: furthest_documented_stage records the most downstream documented stage without bridging an earlier causal gap.
method.reprisal_rule: A reasonable-grounds or sustained reprisal finding supports causal review but does not itself establish every K0 transition, final merits, or psychological state.
method.threat_rule: A communicated restriction or personnel threat may establish a gate action, but a threatened rating or assignment loss does not establish a completed material consequence.
method.nonselection_rule: A non-selection can establish a gate action and consequence without establishing the initial governing explanation, knower reclassification, or explanation mutation.
method.mixed_merits_rule: Where separate misconduct or management evidence exists, the packet must preserve it and may not attribute every action to the protected contradiction.
method.counterpower_rule: A stay, appeal, rescission, or correction is a control fact and does not prove final merits, complete remedy, or universal effectiveness.
method.promotion_rule: No maintainer disposition creates an included K0 event, determines evidence truth, clears publication, assigns psychological motive, or creates a graph edge.

rows.matter: Protected disclosure outside the local chain of command followed by threatened rating and assignment consequences
rows.bounded_domain: An FBI technician’s protected compliance disclosure to an authorized Special Agent in Charge and the home-office response governing outside communications, appraisal standing, and temporary-duty eligibility
rows.qualification_basis: The technician held the relevant technical role, had served the temporary-duty assignment, and made a disclosure that DOJ OIG treated as protected under the FBI Whistleblower Regulations.

source_packets.supports: DOJ OIG found that supervisors lacked adequate training to recognize protected disclosures outside the chain of command and reported direct threats to appraisal and future temporary-duty opportunities.
The official report surface identifies the technician matter and the reasonable-grounds reprisal finding.

The memorandum records a prohibition on additional outside-Division emails without prior approval, threats to lower the performance rating and dry up temporary-duty opportunities, and OIG’s recommendation that OARM order those threats withdrawn or eliminated.

stage_assessments.basis: Home-office management treated communications outside the Division as subject to prior approval and asserted chain-of-command authority over the technician’s disclosure route.
The technician made a protected compliance disclosure to the Special Agent in Charge of the Division where he had served temporary duty; DOJ OIG treated that recipient and disclosure as protected.
In direct response, supervisors treated the protected disclosure as an improper bypass that could count against the technician’s professional appraisal and future assignment standing.
The substantive compliance concern was converted into a chain-of-command and approval problem attributable to the technician’s conduct rather than an issue requiring merits review.

A supervisor prohibited additional outside-Division emails without prior approval and communicated appraisal and temporary-duty threats after consultation with other officials who could direct or recommend personnel actions.

The communication restriction and threats were real and OIG treated them as reprisal, but the public packet does not establish that the appraisal was actually lowered or that a temporary-duty request was denied.
The packet does not show that the technician lost employment, access to the underlying technical evidence, or the ability to continue reporting through every authorized channel.
OIG recommended that OARM order formal withdrawal or elimination of the threats. The public packet does not establish the final OARM disposition, timing, or complete restoration.

counterevidence: The public materials do not disclose the complete technical merits record underlying the technician’s concern.
The personnel penalties described in the packet were threatened; a completed rating reduction or lost temporary-duty assignment is not shown.
OIG’s reasonable-grounds finding was not the final OARM adjudication.
The record identifies multiple supervisors and an administrative officer with different roles and does not establish identical knowledge or motive.
alternative_explanations: a management training failure concerning protected disclosure channels
a good-faith but legally incorrect attempt to enforce internal communication routing
a mixed event combining legitimate supervisory interests with an unlawful response to protected activity
a reprisal event that does not progress to full K0 sensor removal
open_requirements: the final OARM merits and corrective-action disposition
the complete technical concern and management merits response
evidence of any realized appraisal or temporary-duty consequence
independent review of whether the communication restriction materially removed or merely chilled the feedback source

rows.matter: Protected disclosure followed by two non-selections and supervisory intervention in recommendations
rows.bounded_domain: Two FBI selection processes in which supervisors withheld recommendations or altered posting timing after an analyst made protected disclosures
rows.qualification_basis: The analyst occupied the relevant analytical role and made at least one disclosure that DOJ OIG treated as protected under the FBI Whistleblower Regulations.

source_packets.supports: The official report surface identifies the analyst matter and the reasonable-grounds reprisal finding.

OIG found at least one protected disclosure, two non-selections, withheld recommendations that excluded the analyst from consideration, posting timing that made the analyst ineligible, and reasonable grounds to believe reprisal occurred.
The FOIA reading-room surface identifies the underlying February 12, 2020 misconduct report and preserves the distinction between the OIG finding and final OARM adjudication.

stage_assessments.basis: The public summary does not state the supervisors’ pre-action explanation for withholding recommendations, delaying the posting, or preferring other staffing outcomes.
OIG found that the analyst made at least one protected disclosure concerning noncompliance with FBI policies.
The packet documents adverse supervisory conduct but does not quote or otherwise establish a competence, loyalty, attitude, or commitment reclassification of the analyst.
No bounded explanation-before and explanation-after record shows the policy-compliance contradiction being converted into a defect in the analyst.
Supervisors withheld recommendations and manipulated posting timing in ways that excluded the analyst from one competition and made the analyst ineligible for another.
The analyst experienced two non-selections and was deprived of the opportunity to compete on the expected terms.
The packet does not establish loss of the analyst’s job, analytical access, or all protected disclosure channels.
OIG referred the matter to OARM, which held final adjudicative and corrective authority; the public packet does not establish the final disposition or complete remedy.

counterevidence: The OIG reasonable-grounds finding is expressly not the final OARM determination.
The summary does not establish that the analyst was the objectively strongest candidate for either position.
The public packet does not state the supervisors’ contemporaneous merits explanations in sufficient detail to test an explanation mutation.
The underlying FOIA report is a large, partially redacted record and is not represented here as complete exact-byte custody.
alternative_explanations: ordinary selection discretion combined with procedurally improper supervisory conduct
reprisal without a documented epistemic reclassification
staffing and posting decisions with mixed legitimate and retaliatory causes
a personnel-law event outside K0 because the explanation-mutation predicate is absent
open_requirements: the final OARM decision and any corrective action
the supervisors’ contemporaneous explanations for each recommendation and posting decision
evidence of an explicit competence, loyalty, attitude, or commitment reclassification
independent comparative review of candidate qualifications and the two selection records

rows.matter: Congressional testimony followed by loose-cannon and chain-of-command framing, teaching exclusion, proposed discipline, and later suspension
rows.bounded_domain: Neil Jacobs’s congressional testimony concerning missing fraud referrals during CUSA and subsequent INS teaching, discipline, separation, and suspension gates
rows.qualification_basis: Jacobs was Assistant District Director for Investigations with more than 25 years of INS service, recognized operational achievements, and direct responsibility for the fraud-referral function he described.

source_packets.supports: The report records Jacobs’s testimony and qualifications, “disgruntled employee,” “personal agenda,” “loose cannon,” chain-of-command, and reckless-testimony characterizations, attempted teaching exclusion, proposed separation, later suspension, OIG findings that the testimony was generally accurate, and OSC-sustained retaliation.

stage_assessments.basis: INS leadership publicly treated the CUSA complaints as the work of a disgruntled employee with a personal agenda and later characterized Jacobs’s congressional testimony as reckless or in disregard of truth.
Jacobs testified from a senior investigative role that Dallas had effectively produced no routine fraud referrals during CUSA; OIG later found the thrust of his testimony generally accurate.
Managers recoded Jacobs as a disgruntled employee, a loose cannon, a person with an agenda beyond truth-telling, and someone who circumvented the chain of command.
The operational contradiction about missing fraud referrals was converted into a truthfulness, loyalty, recklessness, and chain-of-command defect attributed to Jacobs.
INS attempted to end Jacobs’s professional teaching role, prepared a proposed separation, filed disciplinary charges, and later suspended him.
The teaching approval was initially denied and Jacobs was later suspended; the proposed separation did not issue after OIG intervention.
The suspension removed Jacobs from his INS role for a period, while the attempted teaching exclusion targeted an external professional channel through which his operational standing was expressed.

IACP appeals restored the teaching relationship, OIG intervention stopped the proposed separation, and OSC later sustained retaliation. Those routes supplied correction, but the packet does not establish a timely stay before every consequence or complete restoration.

counterevidence: The OIG report states that Jacobs’s record also supplied grounds that might independently support discipline concerning treatment of subordinates.
Different INS actors made the public statements, teaching decision, proposed separation, and later suspension; common knowledge and motive cannot be presumed.
The IACP teaching relationship was ultimately extended after appeals, and the proposed separation was not sent.
OIG found that INS did not generally retaliate against the many other employees who criticized CUSA, making broad institutional motive unsafe.
alternative_explanations: a mixed case combining protected testimony with independently supportable management concerns
distinct teaching, truthfulness, and subordinate-treatment disputes rather than one unified transaction
ordinary discipline partially contaminated by retaliatory motive
an employment-reprisal case whose K0 fit depends on bounded attribution across several decisionmakers
open_requirements: the OSC disposition and remedy record underlying the sustained retaliation charge
the exact duration and professional effects of the suspension
decisionmaker-specific attribution connecting each explanation to each gate action
independent review separating the testimony-based actions from substantiated subordinate-treatment charges

rows.matter: Situated operational warning met with “just a clerk” and loyalty framing but no substantiated adverse personnel action

source_packets.supports: The report records that managers called Bell “just a clerk,” implied she did not understand the procedures, and viewed her as disloyal, but found no adverse personnel action or prohibited practice caused by her disclosures.

control_findings: The record preserves situated operational knowledge even though the employee held a clerical title.
Managers reportedly questioned Bell’s understanding and loyalty, but OIG found no adverse personnel action caused by her disclosures.
Reclassification language alone does not complete a K0 event without an exercised gate and material consequence.
This control prevents attitude or loyalty language from serving as a substitute for a documented causal chain.

rows.matter: Contractor chain-of-command policy inconsistent with statutory whistleblower protections
rows.institution: U.S. Marshals Service contractor and contract-management system

source_packets.supports: OIG did not substantiate the individual reprisal complaint but found the contractor policy and contract terms inconsistent with statutory whistleblower protections and capable of chilling disclosures.

control_findings: OIG did not substantiate the individual reprisal allegation in the investigated matter.
The contractor policy and contract terms were nevertheless inconsistent with statutory whistleblower protections and capable of chilling disclosure.
A policy-level defect is not one bounded ceiling-conversion event without a qualifying contradiction, reclassification, gate action, and consequence.
This control separates institutional risk architecture from an adjudicated individual event.

rows.matter: Merits standard for lawful discipline labeled insubordination

source_packets.supports: MSPB explains that a misconduct label must be proved and defines insubordination as willful and intentional refusal to obey an authorized order the superior is entitled to have obeyed.
MSPB describes independent appeal routes for removals, suspensions, reductions, and whistleblower claims.

control_findings: An agency that charges insubordination must prove a willful refusal to obey an authorized order the superior was entitled to have obeyed.
Use of a misconduct label does not relieve the agency of proving the underlying conduct and the label’s elements.
Independent appeal architecture exists for covered adverse actions and whistleblower claims, although access and stays are not universal.
Professional disagreement does not immunize refusal of a lawful order and lawful discipline is not a K0 event.

rows.matter: Independent stay halting a whistleblower removal while corrective-action litigation proceeds
rows.institution: U.S. Office of Special Counsel / Merit Systems Protection Board

source_packets.supports: OSC reported an indefinite MSPB stay halting removal after finding strong evidence of retaliation and filing a corrective-action complaint.
MSPB initially granted a 45-day stay based on reasonable grounds to believe protected disclosures contributed to termination.

control_findings: OSC and MSPB can act outside the employing hierarchy to pause a removal while merits litigation continues.
The stay preserves employment standing before the final retaliation decision is complete.
The cited matter progressed from a short stay to an indefinite stay and a corrective-action complaint.
A stay is not a final merits ruling, complete remedy, or proof that this protection is available in every case.

rows.matter: Anti-gag enforcement rescinding chain-of-command restrictions and a reprimand
rows.institution: U.S. Office of Special Counsel and affected federal agencies

source_packets.supports: OSC reported withdrawal or revision of policies forcing all issues through the chain of command and rescission of a VA reprimand that improperly sanctioned an employee for not using official channels.

control_findings: OSC can challenge chain-of-command and nondisclosure restrictions that chill lawful communication with oversight bodies.
The cited enforcement produced rescission of restrictions and correction of an employee record.
The control directly targets the proceduralization move that converts protected disclosure into unauthorized communication.
Observed correction in selected matters does not prove universal access, timely prevention, or final merits in unrelated cases.
